task_description: Help me draft an email to my team about our decision to migrate from REST to gRPC for inter-service communication — we considered GraphQL too but ruled it out.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Writes emails that eliminate the need for follow-up meetings. Every email provides enough context for the reader to understand, decide, and act asynchronously. Values decision transparency and thread hygiene.

rubric.name: Decision Tradeoff Transparency
rubric.description: Emails about decisions include the options that were considered and why the chosen path was selected. Stating a decision without alternatives is an edict, not communication.

dimensions.label: Names at least one alternative that was seriously considered
Explains why each alternative was rejected with specific reasoning, not just 'it didn't fit'
Acknowledges what the chosen option sacrifices compared to alternatives
The decision itself appears in the first two sentences, not after paragraphs of context

rubric.name: Link, Don't Duplicate
rubric.description: Links to existing documents, PRs, dashboards, or design docs replace inline explanations. If information exists somewhere canonical, the email links to it rather than creating a duplicate that will drift.

dimensions.label: References to existing docs, PRs, or dashboards are hyperlinked, not described in prose
Does not reproduce information that's already available at a linked source
Each link has enough surrounding context that the reader knows why to click it

rubric.name: Scoped Review Requests
rubric.description: Review requests specify what kind of feedback is needed and by when. 'Please review' without scope or deadline gets deprioritized — the request must tell the reader exactly what to focus on.

dimensions.label: Specifies the type of feedback requested (architecture, implementation, naming, security, etc.)
Includes a specific deadline or timeframe for the review
Explicitly notes what is NOT in scope for this review round

rubric.name: Thread Discipline
rubric.description: One topic per email thread. If the conversation drifts to a new topic, a new thread with a new subject line is started. Never continues a thread whose subject no longer matches the content.

dimensions.label: The email addresses exactly one topic — does not bundle unrelated items
The subject line accurately describes the current content, not a prior topic in the thread
When introducing a new topic, starts a fresh thread rather than replying to an existing one

rubric_used.coaching_notes: Rachel's philosophy: if someone needs a meeting after reading your email, the email failed. Non-negotiable: decisions always include what was rejected and why. Will push back hard on unbounded review requests or emails that cover multiple topics in one thread.

Subject: Migrating inter-service communication from REST to gRPC

---

Hi team,

**We're moving forward with gRPC for all inter-service communication, starting next sprint.** This replaces our current REST implementation and supersedes the GraphQL evaluation we ran last month.

---

**Why gRPC over the alternatives**

We evaluated three options: keeping REST, adopting GraphQL, and adopting gRPC.

**REST (status quo)** was ruled out because our profiling data showed serialization overhead and the lack of strict contracts are the two largest contributors to the latency issues we've been chasing. REST doesn't solve either problem structurally.

**GraphQL** was a serious contender — schema-first design and strong typing made it attractive. We ruled it out for inter-service use specifically because it's optimized for client-facing, flexible querying, not for high-throughput backend-to-backend calls. It would also introduce a resolver layer with no benefit in our service topology, and our teams don't have existing GraphQL expertise to absorb that ramp-up cost right now.

**gRPC** wins on the two axes that matter most for us: Protobuf serialization is significantly faster and smaller than JSON, and the contract-first `.proto` files give us the strict interface guarantees REST never provided. The tradeoff we're accepting is that gRPC is harder to debug interactively — no curl, no browser inspection. We'll mitigate this with [grpcurl](https://github.com/fullstorydev/grpcurl) and [grpc-gateway](https://github.com/grpc-ecosystem/grpc-gateway) where HTTP fallback is needed.

---

**What this means in practice**

The migration plan, service priority order, and Protobuf style guide are in the [gRPC Migration RFC](#) — that doc has everything you need to start. The tracking board for per-service migration status is [here](#).

I'm not asking anyone to migrate services they don't own; assignments are in the RFC.

---

**One thing I'd like your input on before Friday EOD**

I want a quick gut-check from service owners on the [proposed Protobuf field naming conventions](#) (Section 4 of the RFC). Specifically: does anything conflict with naming patterns already established in your service? I'm not looking for broader architectural feedback on this thread — that window closed with the RFC review last week.

---

Reply here if you have questions. If something is urgent and async won't work, flag it and we'll handle it directly.

Rachel

rounds.draft:
Subject: Migrating inter-service communication from REST to gRPC

---

Hi team,

**We're moving forward with gRPC for all inter-service communication, starting next sprint.** This replaces our current REST implementation and supersedes the GraphQL evaluation we ran last month.

---

**Why gRPC over the alternatives**

We evaluated three options: keeping REST, adopting GraphQL, and adopting gRPC.

**REST (status quo)** was ruled out because our profiling data showed serialization overhead and the lack of strict contracts are the two largest contributors to the latency issues we've been chasing — see the [Q3 Latency Analysis dashboard](#) for the numbers. REST doesn't solve either problem structurally.

**GraphQL** was a serious contender — schema-first design and strong typing made it attractive. We ruled it out for inter-service use specifically because it's optimized for client-facing, flexible querying, not for high-throughput backend-to-backend calls. It would also introduce a resolver layer with no benefit in our service topology, and our teams don't have existing GraphQL expertise to absorb that ramp-up cost right now. Full evaluation is in [Section 2 of the RFC](#).

**gRPC** wins on the two axes that matter most for us: Protobuf serialization is significantly faster and smaller than JSON, and the contract-first `.proto` files give us the strict interface guarantees REST never provided. The tradeoff we're accepting is that gRPC is harder to debug interactively — no curl, no browser inspection. We'll mitigate this with [grpcurl](https://github.com/fullstorydev/grpcurl) and [grpc-gateway](https://github.com/grpc-ecosystem/grpc-gateway) where HTTP fallback is needed.

---

**What this means in practice**

The migration plan, service priority order, and Protobuf style guide are in the [gRPC Migration RFC](#). Rollout assignments and per-service migration status are tracked on the [migration board](#).

---

**One thing I'd like your input on before Friday EOD**

Service owners: please review the [proposed Protobuf field naming conventions](#) in Section 4 of the RFC and answer one specific question: **does anything in Section 4 conflict with naming patterns already established in your service?** A one-line reply per service is enough — I don't need detailed rationale unless there's an actual conflict.

This round is scoped to naming conventions only. Field types, message structure, and broader architecture are not in scope — that window closed with last week's RFC review.

---

This is a new thread. If you have follow-up questions on a different topic — rollout scheduling, tooling setup, or anything else — please start a separate thread so this one stays focused on the migration decision and the naming review.

Reply here if you have questions about the decision or the Section 4 review. If something is urgent and async won't work, flag it and we'll handle it directly.

Rachel
